meta.titre: Modal verbs of obligation: mustn't vs. don't have to

sections.contenu_markdown: 'Mustn't' and 'don't have to' look similar but mean almost opposite things: one forbids, the other simply removes an obligation.

sections.titre: Mustn't vs. don't have to vs. should
sections.contenu_markdown: 'Mustn't' expresses prohibition (it is forbidden to do something); 'don't have to' expresses absence of obligation (it is not necessary, but not forbidden either); 'should' expresses advice or recommendation. The choice depends on whether the context describes a forbidden action or simply an unnecessary one.

sections.enonce_markdown: Complete: 'We ___ go to school on Friday. It is a holiday.'

etapes.justification: A holiday means school is simply not required, not forbidden.
'don't have to' expresses absence of obligation.

sections.conclusion_markdown: "We don't have to go to school on Friday. It is a holiday."

items.erreur_markdown: Using 'mustn't' to mean 'it's not necessary' (a very common confusion, since some languages use a single word for both meanings).
items.pourquoi_faux: 'Mustn't' in English strictly means 'forbidden', while 'don't have to' means 'not necessary' — these are two very different meanings that must not be confused.
items.correction_markdown: Always ask: is the action forbidden (mustn't) or simply unnecessary (don't have to)? A holiday removes obligation, it doesn't forbid attendance.

items.enonce_markdown: Choose the correct modal: 'You ___ smoke in the hospital.' (mustn't / don't have to)
items.solution_markdown: mustn't (smoking in a hospital is forbidden, not merely optional).

items_markdown: don't have to = not necessary (but allowed)
